pos: n. (in the New Testament, the Roman province of proconsular Asia in western Asia Minor, with Ephesus its chief city and the seven churches within it)
etymology: From Greek Asia, the Roman provincial name for the western third of Asia Minor. In Scripture it never means the continent; the boundaries are Roman and administrative, and the KJV keeps the ancient sense.
biblical_def: Asia in the New Testament is a province, not a continent — the western coastland of Asia Minor with Ephesus at its head. It is the field of the most fruitful stretch of Paul's labour. Barred by the Spirit from preaching there on the second journey (Act 16:6), he was later given the whole province at once: teaching daily in the school of Tyrannus, “this continued by the space of two years; so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks” (Act 19:10). Even the silversmiths admitted the scale of it — “almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people” (Act 19:26). Out of that harvest came the seven churches to whom the risen Christ dictates letters: “John to the seven churches which are in Asia” (Rev 1:4). But Asia is also the province of the sharpest sorrow in the epistles. Writing near the end, Paul records a mass defection: “all they which are in Asia be turned away from me” (2Ti 1:15). The same ground gives the dictionary both pictures at once — a whole province hearing the word in two years, and the same province cooling within a generation, with Ephesus itself charged by the Lord to remember whence it had fallen.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Asia as one of the great divisions of the earth; in the New Testament the name denotes the Roman province of that name in Asia Minor.
webster_full: ASIA, n. One of the great continents or quarters of the globe, lying east of Europe and north of the Indian ocean.
In the New Testament the word is used in a narrower sense, for the Roman province of proconsular Asia.
That province comprehended Mysia, Lydia, Caria and part of Phrygia, and its capital was Ephesus.
The seven churches to which the Revelation was addressed were all within this province.
Paul laboured there three years, and all that dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord.
scriptures: And this continued by the space of two years; so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.
Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands:
Rev 1:4
John to the seven churches which are in Asia: Grace be unto you, and peace, from him which is, and which was, and which is to come; and from the seven Spirits which are before his throne;
This thou knowest, that all they which are in Asia be turned away from me; of whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes.
corruption_summary: The rapid evangelization of Asia is copied as a technique, and the equally rapid cooling of Asia is left out of the copy — producing a method for gathering crowds with no doctrine of perseverance attached.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 19 is a favourite text for church-growth strategy: two years, one hall, a whole province reached. What the strategy literature seldom carries over is 2 Timothy 1:15 and Revelation 2:4, where the same province turns away from the apostle and the same flagship church is charged with leaving its first love. The dictionary insists on holding the two together. Paul's own account of his method in Asia was not a technique but a labour: three years of warning “every one night and day with tears” (Act 20:31), and a farewell that predicted grievous wolves entering in among them. A ministry model drawn from the crowds and not from the tears has taken the wrong half.

There is a second and older confusion, harmless in itself but worth naming: reading “Asia” here as the continent. It makes the sentence in Acts 19:10 into something the text does not claim and hands the sceptic an easy charge of exaggeration. Luke is a precise writer using Roman administrative terms exactly as a first-century reader would — Asia beside Mysia, Bithynia, Galatia and Cilicia, each a real jurisdiction with a real boundary. That precision is itself evidence. A later legend-maker would not have known the provincial map well enough to use it so casually and so correctly.
roots_summary: Greek Asia (G773), Asia; Ephesos (G2181), Ephesus; logos (G3056), word; ekklesia (G1577), church, assembly; apostrepho (G654), to turn away.
roots_lines: Greek Asia (G773) — Asia; the Roman province of western Asia Minor, not the continent.
Greek Ephesos (G2181) — Ephesus; its chief city and the base of Paul's three-year labour.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — assembly, church; the seven of Revelation all stood in this province.
Greek apostrepho (G654) — to turn away, desert; the verb of the defection in 2Ti 1:15.
Greek anthupatos (G446) — proconsul, deputy; the officer of a senatorial province such as Asia.
usage: “All they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus” — two years, one province.
“All they which are in Asia be turned away from me” — the same province, one generation.
“The seven churches which are in Asia” — the harvest, addressed by the risen Christ Himself.

pos: n. (the Roman senatorial province covering southern Greece, with Corinth its capital and Athens within it)
etymology: From Greek Achaia, the Roman provincial name for the Peloponnesus and the Greek mainland south of Macedonia. Paul habitually pairs it with Macedonia, the northern province, as the two halves of Greece.
biblical_def: Achaia is southern Greece under Roman administration, and in the New Testament it means chiefly Corinth and Athens. Paul entered it after the Macedonian call, reasoned on Mars' hill, and then settled eighteen months in Corinth, where the Lord told him in a vision that He had much people in that city. The province gave him his most difficult congregation and his most affectionate boasting. Its first converts are named with honour: “ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints” (1Co 16:15). Its generosity toward the poor saints at Jerusalem is held up to shame the Macedonians into action — “Achaia was ready a year ago; and your zeal hath provoked very many” (2Co 9:2) — and then, in the same letter, the Macedonians' poverty is held up to shame Achaia. Both provinces gave (Rom 15:26). Achaia is also where a Roman magistrate refused to make the church a legal question at all: “when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul” (Act 18:12), and Gallio threw the case out, a ruling that sheltered the gospel across the province for years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Achaia; it is the Roman province comprehending the Peloponnesus and southern Greece, with Corinth for its capital.
webster_full: ACHAIA, n. A Roman province, comprehending the Peloponnesus and the southern part of Greece.
Its capital was Corinth, the seat of the proconsul or deputy.
Athens, where Paul disputed in the Areopagus, lay within the same province.
It is commonly named with Macedonia, the two provinces together comprehending all Greece.
The household of Stephanas is called the firstfruits of Achaia.
scriptures: And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat,
I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,)
For I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago; and your zeal hath provoked very many.
For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: Gallio's refusal to judge is praised as a model of religious neutrality, when Luke records it as providence sheltering the gospel; and the Achaian collection is recast as social programme rather than as the fruit of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Gallio is regularly enlisted as an early hero of the secular state — the magistrate who would not adjudicate religion. Luke tells the episode differently. The ruling is not neutrality on principle; it is a Roman official declining a case he considers beneath him, and its effect is to give the church legal cover in a whole province at the moment it most needed it. That is providence, not policy. Scripture's doctrine of the magistrate is not that he is indifferent to God — “he is the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4) — but that Christ governs him whether he confesses it or not, and can shelter His people through a man who cares nothing for them.

The second misreading takes the collection for the poor saints as a charitable programme detachable from doctrine. Paul will not let it be. He grounds the giving in the incarnation itself — “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” (2Co 8:9) — calls the Macedonian generosity “the grace of God bestowed on the churches” (2Co 8:1), and makes the whole business an exercise in provoking one province by the example of another. Mercy toward the poor is not the church's alternative to the gospel; it is what the gospel produces in men who have understood what they were given.
roots_summary: Greek Achaia (G882), Achaia; anthupatos (G446), proconsul, deputy; aparche (G536), firstfruits; charis (G5485), grace; koinonia (G2842), fellowship, contribution.
roots_lines: Greek Achaia (G882) — Achaia; the Roman province of southern Greece.
Greek anthupatos (G446) — proconsul, rendered “deputy”; Gallio's office in Act 18:12.
Greek aparche (G536) — firstfruits; the household of Stephanas, first converts of the province.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace; Paul's name for the giving of the churches in 2Co 8.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, communication, contribution; the collection for Jerusalem.
usage: “The firstfruits of Achaia” — a household named for being first.
“When Gallio was the deputy of Achaia” — a bored magistrate, and a province opened.
“Achaia was ready a year ago” — one church's readiness used to provoke another's.

pos: n. (the Roman province in south-eastern Asia Minor containing Tarsus, the birthplace of the apostle Paul)
etymology: From Greek Kilikia, the coastal region between the Taurus mountains and the sea in south-eastern Asia Minor, joined administratively with Syria in the first century. The KJV keeps the Roman pairing, “Syria and Cilicia”.
biblical_def: Cilicia matters in the New Testament for one reason above all others: it is where Paul came from. He says so twice under pressure, and both times with a certain plainness of pride — “I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city” (Act 21:39), and again before the mob, “born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel” (Act 22:3). The province gave him a Greek city's learning, a Roman citizenship, and a Hebrew household, and God had prepared all three for a work not yet named. Cilicia is also where he went in the silent years. After Damascus and the first flight from Jerusalem, “afterwards I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia” (Gal 1:21) — years of labour of which Acts says almost nothing, and out of which came churches, for when Paul passed through later he “went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches” (Act 15:41). Those congregations were among the first Gentile churches, and the letter from the Jerusalem council was addressed to the brethren in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia by name.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Cilicia; it is the maritime province of south-eastern Asia Minor whose chief city was Tarsus, the birthplace of Paul.
webster_full: CILICIA, n. A province of Asia Minor, lying on the Mediterranean between Pamphylia and Syria.
Its chief city was Tarsus, a seat of learning, and the birthplace of the apostle Paul.
In the Roman administration it was joined with Syria, and the two are named together in the Acts.
Paul laboured there in the years between his conversion and his call to Antioch.
The decree of the council at Jerusalem was addressed to the brethren of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia.
scriptures: But Paul said, I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city: and, I beseech thee, suffer me to speak unto the people.
Act 22:3

I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.
Gal 1:21
Afterwards I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia;
And he went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches.
corruption_summary: Paul's Cilician upbringing is used to make him a Hellenizer who reinvented the religion of Jesus, when he himself cites Tarsus and Gamaliel in the same breath and calls his old zeal a persecution.
corruption_paragraphs: A long-running thesis holds that Paul, a Greek-city Jew from Cilicia, refashioned a simple Galilean faith into a Hellenistic mystery religion — that the gospel of grace and the divine Christ are Tarsus rather than Nazareth. The dictionary rejects it, and Paul's own sentence is the shortest refutation: born in Tarsus, brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, taught “according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers”. He was a Pharisee, trained in Jerusalem by the most respected rabbi of the age. Further, he insists that what he preached he did not invent and did not receive from men — “I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal 1:12) — and the Jerusalem apostles, who had every reason to catch an innovator, gave him the right hands of fellowship.

There is a lesson in the province beyond the controversy. Cilicia holds the hidden years. Between the Damascus road and Antioch lie roughly a decade of labour that Scripture summarizes in a phrase, and a man of Paul's gifts spent it in obscurity in his home region, confirming churches nobody wrote about. The modern instinct is to treat unrecorded years as wasted ones. God's ordinary way is the opposite: Moses in Midian, David among the sheep, the Lord Jesus Himself thirty years in a carpenter's shop. “For who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10).
roots_summary: Greek Kilikia (G2791), Cilicia; Tarsos (G5019), Tarsus; episterizo (G1991), to confirm, strengthen; klima (G2824), region; politeia (G4174), citizenship.
roots_lines: Greek Kilikia (G2791) — Cilicia; the province of south-eastern Asia Minor.
Greek Tarsos (G5019) — Tarsus; its chief city, “no mean city”, and Paul's birthplace.
Greek klima (G2824) — region, district; “the regions of Syria and Cilicia” in Gal 1:21.
Greek episterizo (G1991) — to confirm, establish, strengthen; Paul's work among its churches.
Greek politeia (G4174) — citizenship, commonwealth; the standing Tarsus and Rome gave him.
usage: “A Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city” — a providence assembled before he knew it.
“I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia” — ten years in one line.
“Confirming the churches” — congregations planted in the years nobody recorded.

pos: n. (an inland region of Asia Minor, divided between the Roman provinces of Asia and Galatia, and traversed repeatedly by Paul)
etymology: From Greek Phrugia, an ancient inland district of Asia Minor whose old ethnic name outlived the Roman provincial boundaries drawn across it. Luke uses the popular regional name alongside the administrative ones.
biblical_def: Phrygia is the high inland country of Asia Minor, an old people and an old name that the Romans cut in two when they drew their provinces. Phrygians were among the pilgrims who heard the apostles speak in their own tongues at Pentecost — “Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene” (Act 2:10) — so the word reached the region before any missionary did. Paul crossed it three times. On the second journey, “when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia” they were “forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia” (Act 16:6), a closing of doors that drove them north and finally to the Macedonian vision and to Europe. On the third journey he returned deliberately, going “over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples” (Act 18:23). The two verses set out the whole rhythm of apostolic labour: the Spirit forbids in one place and sends to another, and the same man comes back later to establish what was planted. Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis all lay in Phrygian country, so the epistle to the Colossians is a letter into this region.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Phrygia; it is an inland region of Asia Minor, afterwards divided between the Roman provinces of Asia and Galatia.
webster_full: PHRYGIA, n. An interior region of Asia Minor, bounded by Bithynia, Galatia, Lycaonia, Pisidia, Lydia and Mysia.
Under the Romans it was divided, part being annexed to Asia and part to Galatia.
Phrygians were present at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, and heard the apostles in their own tongue.
Paul passed through the country on his second and third journeys.
Colosse, Laodicea and Hierapolis were cities of Phrygia.
scriptures: Act 2:10
Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome, Jews and proselytes,
Act 16:6
Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia,
And after he had spent some time there, he departed, and went over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples.
Act 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
corruption_summary: The Spirit's forbidding is read as circumstance or as a failure of nerve, and guidance is reduced to an inward impression; Scripture presents it as the sovereign direction of a mission by its Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke says the Holy Ghost forbade them, and the Spirit of Jesus “suffered them not” (Act 16:7). Two ways of dissolving that are common. The first naturalizes it — illness, hostility, closed roads — so that providence replaces the person of the Spirit. The second inflates it into a template, as though every believer should expect audible vetoes before each decision. The dictionary holds the plain reading against both. The Spirit really and personally directed the apostolic mission, because that mission was foundational and was being steered toward Europe by God Himself. Ordinary guidance since is given chiefly through a sufficient Scripture, a sanctified mind, and the counsel of the church — “the meek will he guide in judgment” (Psa 25:9) — and a Christian who waits for a forbidding before obeying a plain command has mistaken the exceptional for the rule.

The second corruption is closer to home: reading a closed door as a defeat. Paul was barred from a province he plainly wanted, and the bar produced the Macedonian call and the gospel in Europe. Nothing in the narrative suggests he understood it at the time. The believer's confidence is not that he can read the providence while he is inside it, but that the God who writes it is good and cannot be thwarted: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). Asia was not refused him for ever — three years in Ephesus were coming. It was refused him then.
roots_summary: Greek Phrugia (G5435), Phrygia; koluo (G2967), to forbid, hinder; dierchomai (G1330), to pass through; episterizo (G1991), to strengthen; horama (G3705), vision.
roots_lines: Greek Phrugia (G5435) — Phrygia; the inland region of Asia Minor.
Greek koluo (G2967) — to forbid, hinder, withstand; the Spirit's act in Act 16:6.
Greek dierchomai (G1330) — to go through, traverse; the verb of the apostolic itineraries.
Greek episterizo (G1991) — to confirm, strengthen; the purpose of the third-journey return.
Greek horama (G3705) — vision, sight; the Macedonian man seen in the night at Troas.
usage: “Forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia” — a closed door with a purpose behind it.
“Strengthening all the disciples” — the apostle goes back to the ground he crossed.
“Phrygia, and Pamphylia” — the word arrived at Pentecost before the missionary did.

pos: n. (the north-western district of Asia Minor, through which Paul passed on his way to Troas and Europe)
etymology: From Greek Musia, the north-western corner of Asia Minor, within the Roman province of Asia. Luke names it twice in two verses and never again — it is a place passed through, not preached in.
biblical_def: Mysia occupies two verses of Scripture and both of them are about movement. Barred from Asia, Paul and Silas came up to the northern edge of the province: “After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not” (Act 16:7). Blocked a second time, they had one direction left. “And they passing by Mysia came down to Troas” (Act 16:8) — and at Troas came the vision of the man of Macedonia, and the gospel crossed into Europe. Mysia is therefore the hinge of the most consequential turn in the book of Acts, and nothing at all is said to have happened there. No church is planted, no sermon recorded, no convert named. It is the ground a man walks across when two doors have shut and he does not yet know why. Luke's pronoun changes at Troas — “immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia” (Act 16:10) — the physician joins the party, and the narrative that carries the gospel to Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth and finally Rome begins on the far side of this unremarkable district.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Mysia; it is the north-western district of Asia Minor, lying between Bithynia and the province of Asia, with Troas on its coast.
webster_full: MYSIA, n. A district in the north-west of Asia Minor, within the Roman province of Asia.
It was bounded by Bithynia on the east and the Aegean sea on the west.
Troas, where Paul saw the vision of the man of Macedonia, lay on its coast.
Paul and Silas passed by Mysia, being forbidden to enter Bithynia.
No church is recorded to have been planted within it at that time.
scriptures: Act 16:7
After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not.
Act 16:8
And they passing by Mysia came down to Troas.
Act 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
Act 16:6
Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia,
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that God ordinarily governs His servants through refusals, and that ground crossed without visible fruit is not ground wasted.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Mysia is a place-name in a travel narrative and carries no doctrinal freight that anyone has troubled to distort. What it does carry is a lesson the church needs restated in every generation: that the Lord leads His servants as much by shutting doors as by opening them, and that the shutting is not punishment. Two provinces were refused Paul in a fortnight. He did not sulk, did not force the door, and did not stop walking; he went where he could go, and at the end of the road that was left him he found the vision that redirected the mission of the church.

The principle to recover is patience under unexplained providence. Modern Christians are taught to expect a sense of confirmation before each step and to read the absence of it as a sign that God has withdrawn. Scripture teaches obedience in the dark: “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5). Mysia was crossed in that spirit — a stretch of road with no sermon in it, walked by men who had just been told no twice, and it was the shortest way to Europe. The Christian who has been refused twice this year is standing where the apostles stood, and should keep walking.

roots_lines: Greek Musia (G3465) — Mysia; the north-western district of Asia Minor.
Greek peirazo (G3985) — to try, attempt, assay; they assayed to go into Bithynia.
Greek eao (G1439) — to suffer, allow, permit; “the Spirit suffered them not”.
Greek parerchomai (G3928) — to pass by, pass along; their route past Mysia to the coast.
Greek Troas (G5174) — Troas; the port where the Macedonian vision was given.
usage: “They assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not” — the second closed door in a fortnight.
“Passing by Mysia came down to Troas” — the road left open when the others shut.
A district with no church in it, and Europe on the other side.

pos: n. (a Roman province on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor, refused to Paul by the Spirit and later addressed by Peter)
etymology: From Greek Bithunia, the province along the southern shore of the Black Sea and the Propontis. It is named twice in the New Testament, once as a door shut and once as a field already harvested.
biblical_def: Bithynia is the province Paul was not allowed to enter. Standing at the border of Mysia he “assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not” (Act 16:7), and he turned west to Troas and to Europe instead. That is the whole of Bithynia in Acts — a refusal. But the New Testament does not leave it there, and the second mention is one of the quiet glories of Scripture. Peter opens his first epistle: “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1Pe 1:1). There are churches in Bithynia. Someone reached them — Scripture never says who, and the silence is the point. The province forbidden to the greatest missionary in the history of the church was evangelized by men whose names are not recorded, and within a generation there were enough believers there to be addressed by an apostle as elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father. The work of God is not confined to the workers we can name, and a field closed to one servant is not closed to the Lord of the harvest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Bithynia; it is a province of Asia Minor on the Euxine sea, named in the Acts and in the first epistle of Peter.
webster_full: BITHYNIA, n. A province of Asia Minor, bordering on the Euxine or Black sea and the Propontis.
Paul and Silas assayed to go thither, but the Spirit suffered them not.
It is named among the regions to whose scattered strangers Peter directed his first epistle.
Churches therefore existed within it, though the Acts records no mission to the province.
It adjoined Mysia on the west and Pontus and Galatia on the east and south.
scriptures: Act 16:7
After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not.
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,
Act 16:8
And they passing by Mysia came down to Troas.
Act 16:6
Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia,
corruption_summary: The apostolic mission is treated as though the church's growth depended on named apostles, when Scripture itself records flourishing churches in a province no recorded missionary entered.
corruption_paragraphs: Church history is often written as a chain of great men, and the New Testament is read to match — Paul plants, Peter presides, and the growth of the church is the sum of apostolic itineraries. Bithynia refutes the model from inside the canon. Paul was forbidden to enter it; no missionary journey to it is recorded anywhere; and by the time Peter writes there are congregations there substantial enough to be addressed as a body. The gospel travelled by merchants, soldiers, slaves and household servants whose names appear in no list. That is the ordinary way it has always travelled. Paul himself refused the great-man frame: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6).

The second corruption is a pastoral one: reading a refusal as a rejection of the field. Paul was kept out of Bithynia, and Bithynia was saved. The believer whose plan is blocked is tempted to conclude that the thing he wanted was not God's will at all, or worse, that God does not care for it. Scripture allows a better reading — that the LORD may love a work and simply not have assigned it to you. David desired to build the house and was told his son would build it; the desire was commended and the office refused. “Whereas it was in thine heart to build an house unto my name, thou didst well that it was in thine heart” (1Ki 8:18).
roots_summary: Greek Bithunia (G978), Bithynia; parepidemos (G3927), stranger, sojourner; diaspora (G1290), dispersion; eklektos (G1588), elect; eao (G1439), to suffer, permit.
roots_lines: Greek Bithunia (G978) — Bithynia; the Black Sea province of northern Asia Minor.
Greek parepidemos (G3927) — sojourner, resident alien; Peter's word for his readers there.
Greek diaspora (G1290) — dispersion, scattering; the condition of the churches he addresses.
Greek eklektos (G1588) — chosen, elect; how Peter names them in his opening sentence.
Greek eao (G1439) — to suffer, permit; the verb of the Spirit's refusal in Act 16:7.
usage: “They assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not” — the door shut.
“Scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” — the door opened by someone else.
A province Paul never entered, full of saints before he died.

pos: n. (the Roman province along the southern shore of the Black Sea; home of Aquila, and first-named in Peter's address to the scattered elect)
etymology: From Greek Pontos, sea — the region taking its name from the Euxine, the Black Sea, on whose southern coast it lay. The Latin name preserves the Greek word for the water itself.
biblical_def: Pontus lies on the far northern rim of the world the New Testament knows, and it appears three times, each time with weight out of proportion to the mention. Men of Pontus were in Jerusalem at Pentecost and heard the wonderful works of God in their own tongue — the list begins “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites… in Pontus, and Asia” (Act 2:9). Second, it gave the church one of its most valuable couples: “a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla” (Act 18:2), expelled from Rome by Claudius, met by Paul in Corinth, tentmakers who housed him, worked beside him, followed him to Ephesus and there took Apollos aside and expounded the way of God more perfectly. Third and last, Peter heads his address with it: “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1Pe 1:1). The trajectory is worth marking. A province at the edge of the map sends pilgrims to Pentecost, receives the word, exports a craftsman couple who become pillars of two churches, and within a generation holds congregations addressed by an apostle as “elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father” (1Pe 1:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Pontus; it is a province of Asia Minor on the southern coast of the Euxine or Black sea.
webster_full: PONTUS, n. A country and Roman province of Asia Minor, lying along the Euxine sea.
The name is the Greek word for the sea, taken from the water on which it borders.
Men of Pontus were at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.
Aquila, the fellow labourer of Paul, was a Jew born in Pontus.
Peter addresses his first epistle to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus and the neighbouring provinces.
scriptures: Act 2:9
Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia,
Act 18:2
And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them.
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,
Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied.
corruption_summary: Peter's opening words are softened so that election becomes God's response to foreseen faith, and Priscilla's teaching of Apollos is enlisted to overturn what Paul says about the eldership.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter calls the believers of Pontus “elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father”, and the standard softening makes foreknowledge mean advance information — God saw who would believe and chose accordingly. That reading empties the word. In Scripture God's foreknowing of persons is His setting of love upon them beforehand, not His prediction of their behaviour: “whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom 8:29), and the objects are people, not facts about people. Election that depends on foreseen faith is election that depends on the creature, and it cannot be squared with a sentence that grounds the choosing in the Father, the sanctifying in the Spirit, and the obedience in the sprinkled blood of the Son.

The second corruption uses a Pontic couple to unsettle the New Testament's order for the church. Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos and “expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly” (Act 18:26), and the episode is offered as proof that Paul's restriction of the teaching office to men is cultural. It proves nothing of the sort. This is a married couple, together, instructing one man privately in their own household — not a woman holding the office of elder in a congregation. The dictionary holds the plain apostolic rule (1Ti 2:12; 1Ti 3:1-7) alongside the plain apostolic esteem for Priscilla, whom Paul calls his helper in Christ Jesus and thanks by name. Both stand; neither cancels the other.
roots_summary: Greek Pontos (G4195), Pontus; prognosis (G4268), foreknowledge; eklektos (G1588), elect; skenopoios (G4635), tentmaker; diaspora (G1290), dispersion.
roots_lines: Greek Pontos (G4195) — Pontus; the province named from the sea it borders.
Greek prognosis (G4268) — foreknowledge; in Scripture God's prior setting of love, not bare prediction.
Greek eklektos (G1588) — chosen, elect; the standing of the saints in this province.
Greek skenopoios (G4635) — tentmaker; the trade Aquila of Pontus shared with Paul.
Greek parepidemos (G3927) — sojourner, stranger; Peter's name for the scattered believers.
usage: “A certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus” — an exile who became a pillar.
“Strangers scattered throughout Pontus” — the edge of the map, full of the elect.
“In Pontus, and Asia” — the far province present at Pentecost.

pos: n. (a large inland Roman province of eastern Asia Minor, represented at Pentecost and addressed by Peter)
etymology: From Greek Kappadokia, the highland province of eastern Asia Minor. It appears only twice in Scripture, and both mentions place it among peoples receiving the word.
biblical_def: Cappadocia is high inland country in the east of Asia Minor, and Scripture names it exactly twice. The first is Pentecost, in Luke's roll of the nations gathered at Jerusalem: “the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia” (Act 2:9). The second is Peter's address: “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1Pe 1:1). Between those two verses lies a generation of unrecorded labour. No apostle is said to have gone there; no church-planting narrative survives; and yet by the time Peter writes there are believers in Cappadocia enough to receive a circular letter about suffering, holiness and the elder's duty to feed the flock. That letter tells us what kind of Christians they were expected to be: strangers and pilgrims abstaining from fleshly lusts (1Pe 2:11), honouring the emperor who would soon be burning them, and rejoicing to be partakers of Christ's sufferings. The province is a standing witness that the church spread far faster and further than the narrative portions of the New Testament stop to record.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Cappadocia; it is a large inland province of eastern Asia Minor, named at Pentecost and in the first epistle of Peter.
webster_full: CAPPADOCIA, n. A province in the eastern part of Asia Minor, bounded by Pontus, Galatia, Cilicia and Armenia.
It was a high inland country, famed in antiquity for its horses and its flocks.
Dwellers in Cappadocia were at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.
Peter names it among the provinces to whose scattered strangers he wrote.
The Acts records no missionary journey into the province, yet churches were found there.
scriptures: Act 2:9
Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia,
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,
Act 2:10
Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome, Jews and proselytes,
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
corruption_summary: The silence of Acts about provinces like Cappadocia is treated as evidence that the church's early spread is legendary, when it is simply evidence that Acts is a selective history and says so.
corruption_paragraphs: Because no mission to Cappadocia is narrated, the presence of churches there is sometimes offered as a seam in the record — a sign that the epistolary addresses are later idealizations. The inference misreads what kind of book Acts is. Luke tells one line of the story, the line running from Jerusalem through Antioch and Paul to Rome, and he never claims to tell more. John says the same of his own Gospel: “there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books” (Joh 21:25). A selective history is not a false one. The dictionary holds Acts to be accurate in all it reports and incomplete by design.

There is also a corruption of expectation to name, and Cappadocia is a good place to name it. Peter writes to these unrecorded churches about fiery trial, submission under unjust masters, and the glory that follows suffering — not about growth, influence or cultural standing. The therapeutic register that dominates much modern Christian speech would find the letter unusable. Its assumption throughout is that the normal Christian condition in this world is that of a stranger, and that the comfort offered is not relief from affliction but an inheritance “incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away” (1Pe 1:4).
roots_summary: Greek Kappadokia (G2587), Cappadocia; parepidemos (G3927), pilgrim, sojourner; peirasmos (G3986), trial, temptation; kleronomia (G2817), inheritance; diaspora (G1290), dispersion.
roots_lines: Greek Kappadokia (G2587) — Cappadocia; the inland province of eastern Asia Minor.
Greek parepidemos (G3927) — pilgrim, resident alien; the standing Peter assigns his readers.
Greek peirasmos (G3986) — trial, proving; the fiery trial the epistle prepares them for.
Greek kleronomia (G2817) — inheritance; incorruptible, undefiled, reserved in heaven for them.
Greek diaspora (G1290) — dispersion; the scattering through which the gospel travelled.
usage: “And Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia” — the far provinces at Pentecost.
“Strangers scattered throughout… Cappadocia” — churches nobody wrote the founding of.
“Strangers and pilgrims” — the settled expectation of the apostolic letters.

pos: n. (an inland district of Asia Minor containing Lystra and Derbe, where Paul was taken for a god and then stoned)
etymology: From Greek Lukaonia, the inland plain of southern Asia Minor. Luke notes that its people kept their own tongue — “the speech of Lycaonia” — distinct from the Greek in which Paul had just spoken.
biblical_def: Lycaonia is the district of Lystra and Derbe, and it stages one of the most instructive scenes in Acts. Driven from Iconium, “they fled unto Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about” (Act 14:6). There Paul healed a man crippled from birth, and the crowd drew the conclusion their own religion supplied: “when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men” (Act 14:11). They called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercurius and brought oxen and garlands to the gates. The apostles tore their clothes and ran in among them, and what they preached to raw pagans is worth marking — not the covenants, but creation and providence: turn from these vanities to the living God, who made heaven and earth and gave you rain and fruitful seasons (Act 14:15-17). Within days the same crowd, worked on by hostile Jews from Antioch and Iconium, stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city for dead (Act 14:19). Adoration and murder from one crowd in one week. And out of Lycaonia came Timothy (Act 16:1), so the province that nearly killed Paul gave him his dearest son in the faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Lycaonia; it is an inland district of Asia Minor whose cities were Lystra, Derbe and Iconium, and whose people had their own speech.
webster_full: LYCAONIA, n. An inland region of Asia Minor, bordering upon Cappadocia, Galatia, Phrygia, Pisidia and Cilicia.
Its principal cities named in the Acts are Lystra and Derbe.
The inhabitants retained a native tongue, called the speech of Lycaonia.
There Paul and Barnabas were taken for Mercurius and Jupiter, and sacrifice was prepared to them.
There also Paul was stoned and drawn out of the city, and there Timothy was found.
scriptures: Act 14:6
They were ware of it, and fled unto Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about:
And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men.

And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:
And there came thither certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the people, and, having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead.
corruption_summary: The refusal of worship at Lystra is treated as ancient modesty rather than as doctrine, while the same instinct that deified two travellers is alive wherever a preacher is exalted above his message.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul and Barnabas ran in among the crowd tearing their clothes, and the reason they gave was doctrinal, not modest: “We also are men of like passions with you”. That sentence is the whole of the biblical doctrine of the minister. He is not a mediator, not a channel of grace in himself, not a man of a different order; there is “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). The dictionary names as corruption every system that reverses this — the veneration of saints, the priest who stands between, the modern celebrity ministry with its untouchable platform. The Lycaonian error is not extinct; it has changed its vocabulary. And it is a fearful thing that men who accepted such honour in Acts came to bad ends: Herod took the shout “It is the voice of a god, and not of a man” and was eaten of worms (Act 12:22-23).

The second thing to notice is the sermon. To a pagan crowd with no Scripture, Paul does not begin with Moses; he begins with the Creator, the rain, the fruitful seasons, and the witness God has left of Himself in every man's food and gladness. Modern evangelism often assumes a hearer who already grants the categories — sin, judgment, a personal God — and is confused when he does not. Paul assumed nothing and started at Genesis 1. Where a culture has forgotten that it is made, the first work of preaching is not comfort but creation: “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Gen 1:1).
roots_summary: Greek Lukaonia (G3071), Lycaonia; Lukaonisti (G3072), in the speech of Lycaonia; homoiopathes (G3663), of like passions; mataios (G3152), vain, empty; lithazo (G3034), to stone.
roots_lines: Greek Lukaonia (G3071) — Lycaonia; the inland district of Lystra and Derbe.
Greek Lukaonisti (G3072) — in the Lycaonian tongue; Luke's note that the crowd spoke its own speech.
Greek homoiopathes (G3663) — of like passions, of the same nature; the apostles' refusal of worship.
Greek mataios (G3152) — vain, empty, futile; “these vanities” from which they were to turn.
Greek lithazo (G3034) — to stone; what the same crowd did to Paul within days.
usage: “The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men” — paganism's reflex before a miracle.
“We also are men of like passions with you” — the whole doctrine of the ministry in nine words.
“Having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city” — the same crowd, the same week.

pos: n. (the Roman province on the eastern Adriatic, named by Paul as the furthest bound of his preaching)
etymology: From Latin Illyricum, the province along the eastern shore of the Adriatic north-west of Macedonia. Paul names it once, as a boundary marker rather than a destination.
biblical_def: Illyricum appears once in Scripture, in a sentence Paul writes to summarize his life's work: “so that from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum, I have fully preached the gospel of Christ” (Rom 15:19). It is a boundary, not a stop — the north-western limit of the arc he had swept, running up the Adriatic coast beyond Macedonia. The claim in the sentence is remarkable and precise. He does not say every soul between those points had been converted, but that he had fully preached — fulfilled, filled out — the gospel across that whole region, so that he no longer had place there and was free to look toward Spain. Two verses later he explains the principle that governed the whole itinerary: “so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation” (Rom 15:20). That is a deliberate policy of going to the unreached, held by a man who could have spent his life pastoring the churches he had already planted. Illyricum is where the compass needle of that policy pointed at the end of the third journey, and the reason Romans exists at all is that he intended to pass through Rome on his way further west.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Illyricum; it is a Roman province on the eastern coast of the Adriatic, named by Paul as the limit of his preaching.
webster_full: ILLYRICUM, n. A Roman province lying along the eastern shore of the Adriatic sea.
It bordered upon Macedonia on the south and reached northward toward Pannonia.
Paul declares that from Jerusalem round about unto Illyricum he had fully preached the gospel.
The name marks the north-western boundary of his labours in the east.
Dalmatia, whither Titus afterward departed, lay within the same region.
scriptures: Through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God; so that from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum, I have fully preached the gospel of Christ.
Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation:
For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem.
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
corruption_summary: Paul's claim to have fully preached from Jerusalem to Illyricum is either inflated into a promise that every region will be evangelized in a generation, or deflated into apostolic exaggeration.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern missions strategy has sometimes read Romans 15:19 as a template with a timetable — a region declared reached, a task closed, the Lord's return hastened by completing the map. Paul's own claim is more careful than that. He says he has no more place in those parts, meaning the gospel has been established there with churches and elders and a witness that will carry on without him; he does not say the work in those provinces is finished, and he keeps writing letters to them for the rest of his life. The dictionary honours the missionary urgency in the verse and declines the mechanical reading. The Great Commission is a command to disciple the nations, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever Christ commanded (Mat 28:20) — a work of generations, not a checklist.

The opposite corruption treats the sentence as rhetoric — a tired apostle rounding up. That reading has to ignore the sober company the claim keeps. In the same letter Paul lists his sufferings, refuses to boast in another man's labour, asks for prayer that he may be delivered from unbelievers in Judaea, and admits that his service may not be accepted. He is not a man given to inflation. And the signs and wonders he cites are attributed not to himself but to the power of the Spirit of God. When such a man says he has fully preached Christ from Jerusalem to the Adriatic, the sentence should be believed.
roots_summary: Greek Illurikon (G2437), Illyricum; pleroo (G4137), to fill, fulfil, fully preach; philotimeomai (G5389), to strive, make it one's ambition; themelios (G2310), foundation; euaggelizo (G2097), to preach the gospel.
roots_lines: Greek Illurikon (G2437) — Illyricum; the Adriatic province marking the limit of Paul's arc.
Greek pleroo (G4137) — to fill up, complete, fulfil; behind “I have fully preached”.
Greek philotimeomai (G5389) — to be ambitious, to strive earnestly; his policy in Rom 15:20.
Greek themelios (G2310) — foundation; what he refused to build upon when another had laid it.
Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to announce good news, preach the gospel; the verb of his whole life.
usage: “From Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum” — a life's work measured on a map.
“I have fully preached the gospel of Christ” — filled it out, not merely announced it.
“Not where Christ was named” — a deliberate policy of going where no one had gone.
